item.title: Your chaotic Google Messages group chats might finally get threaded replies
item.dc:content:
Google Messages might be getting a much-needed upgrade that could make long conversations much easier to follow.

Google is said to be working on a feature called threaded replies, which will enable users to keep conversations tied to a specific message, rather than having replies scattered around an increasingly chaotic chat, as spotted by the folks at Android Authority. It’s particularly handy for group conversations, where several people can be talking about different things simultaneously, and nobody knows which message they’re actually replying to.

The current setup isn’t really suited for conversations that split into a few smaller ones. Google Messages displays a preview of the original message above each reply, but it can get confusing after a long exchange when unrelated messages begin appearing between responses.

Google’s proposed fix appears to be visually linking related messages. In the chat bubbles, you’ll see a vertical line on the left side that will show which messages are grouped together. A single reply is a straight connecting line; longer exchanges with multiple replies have a small loop in the line. The system works with images and emojis along with text.

Furthermore, Google is also adding reply counters beneath messages in active conversations. That counter can be tapped, and Messages will open a dedicated thread view. The other conversation fades into the background, and you only see the related messages. You have a separate reply box to continue the conversation, as well as an X button to go back to the main conversation.

This should make it much less frustrating to catch up on busy group chats. You can jump right into the conversation that matters, without having to scroll through dozens of unrelated messages to get the context of someone’s reply.

Google is still borrowing from Apple's playbook

The similarities to Apple’s iMessage are difficult to ignore. Apple already has threaded conversations that split out replies from the main chat, and Google seems to be doing something similar. That’s not necessarily a bad thing, though. Messaging apps should strive to make conversations easier to follow, regardless of who first brought an idea up.

For now, threaded replies are an experimental feature hidden in the development code of Google Messages. Google hasn’t announced a release date, and there’s no guarantee the feature will make it to the stable version. But its relatively polished implementation suggests the company is making meaningful strides.

item.title: Razr 2027 leak: earlier launch, and Moto might deliver upgrades that matter
item.dc:content:
Foldables continue to gather steam. Motorola's next wave of 2027 foldables is expected; however, a rumor suggests we might see them earlier.

This morning (Nov. 24), an Android Headlines report alleged what the Motorola Razr 2027 could look like. Rumors suggest upgrades for Moto's 2027 foldable, and it looks like what we were hoping for. The publication alleges the Razr 2027 will finally get rid of the ugly border on its cover display. This has been there since its display was smaller; however, rumors say it could feature a 4-inch cover screen.

A leaked render claims this would expand the Razr 2027's cover display to its hinge, mirroring a Galaxy Z Flip 8 experience or a Razr Ultra. Elsewhere, the leak claims Motorola wants to boost its battery cell. The Razr 2027 could feature a 5,000mAh cell, a 200mAh upgrade from the 2026 variant's 4,800mAh. The foldable's charging might also increase to 45W (up from 30W).

Since these rumors discuss the base Razr model for 2027, Motorola's chip of choice was a hot topic. It seems Motorola will stick with MediaTek's mid-range Dimensity chip line next year. It's not a terrible thing, but given the price of the Razr 2026, which the 2027 version might not be far from, the chosen chip could be better.

Internally, the 8GB of RAM and 256GB of stroage could grace the next Razr. If these rumors sound exciting, they suggest we might not have to wait long. Supposedly, Motorola is gearing up to reveal its Razr 2027 during CES 2027 in early January.

Moto's finally doing work

Android Central's Take

Our wants and desires for the Razr 2027 also mentioned a "mid-range Razr." What we meant was a true mid-range Razr. I agree with this. It'd be nice if all of the Razrs had a stronger, more powerful chip. It kind of sucks having this weaker chip on an otherwise nice foldable phone.

This is a substantial leak, and it's got us thinking back to our original wants and desires for the Razr 2027. The 2026 version wasn't that exciting. It was a decent foldable, yes, but Motorola's "upgrades" weren't all that better. One upgrade we wanted was 256GB of stroage. It's nice to see this rumored, but we need it to actually happen. This year's model cut its storage in half while somehow still increasing its price. It was a distasteful change compared to the 2025 version.

Another area we wanted Motorola to do better in was software upgrades. The 2026 model will only receive three years of OS upgrades and five years of security patches. Unfortunately, according to the publication, that might not change. It sucks when you consider what Google and Samsung are doing: a seven-year promise.

We can't forget to mention Motorola's work with GrapheneOS. This privacy-first software is set to arrive on a selection of Moto phones in 2027. Foldables are on the list, but they will come after. Moreover, you might only see GrapheneOS appear on the Razr Ultra and Fold.
item.description: The Moto Razr 2027 sounds like a foldable worth your attention after this leak. It might launch earlier next year, too—like, really early.

item.title: The Ear Note is Nothing's AI device with a recording case—December launch confirmed
item.dc:content:
AI is everywhere, and now we're getting a closer look at an AI-focused device from Nothing. The company teased it recently, and it might've gone the way you expected.

This week, Mark Gurman from Bloomberg (paywall) sat down with Nothing's CEO, Carl Pei, to discuss what the future holds for its AI device (via GSMArena). First, Gurman teased the device on X, saying the Nothing Ear (Note) is a pair of earbuds "that record and transcribe both in-person meetings and phone calls." Their conversation then shifted to the Ear Note's charging case.

The charging case looks like a proper case (or an old-school cassette recorder). This early glimpse highlighted something familiar: a massive "TALK" button. Pressing "TALK" reportedly lets users record themselves or what's going on around them through the case. While the case is more "external," the earbuds can record phone calls.

Users can also expect transcription. However, this is likely available through the Ear Note companion app. Ear Note will support summaries of previous conversations/recordings, as well as "various AI agents." Carl Pei added more context on X. Pei said, "AI is only as useful as what it knows about you. This is the first of many products building a hardware context layer for AI."

The Nothing Ear Note is preparing to launch on December 8. Privacy has been a concern (for users, as well as Nothing), and it was reported that the company integrated safeguards.

Thoughts, questions, concerns?

We should've expected a device with some retro vibes after Carl Pei's teaser earlier this month. Pei gave a small glimpse of Nothing's "screenless AI device." He showed the Ear Note's (as we've come to know it) red and green LED indicators. Pei also said, "context doesn't live in a chat box." The teaser was kept extremely brief ahead of Pei's interview with Bloomberg.

His X post added, "It has no new screen, and it couldn't have been an app." This is interesting because users on social media have likened it to the Essential Recorder app on Nothing phones. It certainly feels similar, but that's because we're trading in one recording app for recording functionality on a pair of earbuds and a case. December 8 will answer everything else we're curious about.

Android Central's Take

I've seen people on social media question why this device exists. I've already called out the Essential Recorder app, as others did on X. Users on Reddit and X also raise privacy concerns. People are curious whether the Ear Note will let them know they're being recorded. Consent is a huge thing, and rightfully so. Personally, I don't necessarily see the need for this. People have joked that this would only be useful for people "constantly hopping between meetings." Even then, I'd rather jot down some quick notes.

item.title: I bought both the Echo Spot and Echo Time smart speakers – and there’s only one I’m keeping on my nightstand this Black Friday
item.dc:content:
As someone who devours live radio and podcasts, there's no smart home item I love more than a bedside smart speaker. I've owned loads of different models over the years, including options from Lenovo, Google, and, of course, Amazon, but my most recent upgrade involved swapping out my reliable Echo Spot in favor of the new Echo Time.

I bought both speakers for full price on their respective launch days, and have had plenty of time to test the two models and really get to grips with the many differences between them. Whether you should go with the Echo Spot or Echo Time is likely going to be a big question this Black Friday. After all, the Echo Spot has dropped to just $44.99 (down from $109.99) as part of the sale, while the Echo Time has fallen to $99.99 (from $199.99) thanks to a mega 50% off discount.

But is the Echo Time actually worth double the cost? Here's everything you need to know about the two models, and my take on which is the better pick in the ongoing sales.

  • Browse all the latest Black Friday Amazon deals

The Amazon Echo Spot is the better pick if you want a basic, distraction-free listening experience. It features a small screen that's used for little more than displaying a clock face and showing some simple animations. Of course, as an Alexa speaker, you can also ask it for the weather, to tell fun jokes, or set alarms.View Deal

✅Recommended if: You want a simple, no-nonsense smart speaker for your nightstand. The Echo Spot has a compact display that is used to show you the time and, occasionally, a basic animation or two. It's the ideal model if you want something that functions like a standard clock, but with the added smart-speaker functionality of Alexa.

❌Skip this deal if: You're after a more advanced, customizable bedside companion with better sound. I frequently found myself frustrated by the limitations of the Echo Spot, particularly the limited number of very basic clock faces that you can choose from. The Echo Time blows it away in terms of customizability. The Time also sounds better, with more detailed and rich audio.

Better sound and more customization

The newer Echo Time offers richer and more detailed sound than the Spot. It's also much more customizable, with a wide range of clock face options that you can tweak to your liking. The larger screen dims at night, so it doesn't keep you awake, and gently illuminates in the morning to help you wake up. In my eyes, all of this is well worth the extra $55 if you have the budget.View Deal

✅Recommended if: You want an all-round, more advanced bedside companion. While the Echo Spot was released back in 2024, the Echo Time came out earlier this year – and you can really tell, given just how much more advanced it is than its predecessor. It boasts a large, round display that you can customize with a wide range of clock faces, as well as noticeably upgraded sound that's both richer and more detailed.

I also think the design looks and feels much more premium in your home. The Echo Spot has a matte plastic finish and a basic cloth cover over its speaker grille, while the Echo Spot is covered with this lovely woven material all over.

❌Skip this deal if: You think the Echo Spot will meet your needs. If you are simply after a small screen that can display the time and decent, but not exceptional, sound, you will most likely still be able to make do with the more basic Spot – and save yourself some cash in the process.

item.title: I compared the heavily discounted Echo Dot Max and 5th Gen Echo Dot to find out which is the best deal this Black Friday
item.dc:content:
Amazon has won the smart home Olympics with its range of Echo devices, but it's tricky to settle on one when there are so many options out there — and the Black Friday madness doesn't help, either.

There are two star devices in Amazon's Black Friday event: the 5th-gen Echo Dot and the newer Echo Dot Max, both of which are some of the best smart speakers out there. On a regular day, you'd be paying the best part of $100 for each, but the current Black Friday offers are hard to ignore.

As for the previous-gen model, the Echo Dot is now $39.99 down from $79.99, while the upgraded Echo Dot Max is $49.99 down from $199.99. So what's the difference between the two devices, and how do you decide which one is best for you?

Similarities-wise, both are compact smart speakers that any bookcase, media unit, or countertop can adorn. Both support Amazon's upgraded AI voice assistant, Alexa+, and both speakers have fine-tuned inner workings that boost mighty audio performance - but the Echo Dot Max's upgrades could be the reason you spend a little more.

Though the 5th-gen Echo Dot is far from a poor smart hub, its newer sibling is more advanced not only on the audio side, but also on the smart home front, which you can dive into below. For those who aren't too fussed with getting all the bells and whistles, the Echo Dot is plenty to get you by, but for just $10 extra you'll be getting a lot more — I know which one I'd be spending my money on this Black Friday.

  • Browse all the latest Black Friday Amazon deals

Echo Dot (5th-Gen): was $79.99 now $39.99
It's not the lowest price we've seen for this Echo device, but who can say no to a $40 smart speaker? It's compact, fits nicely in any room, and doesn't fall flat on offering a bold audio experience. Despite being a previous gen model, it's a top pick for us, and one we always keep an eye out for during Black Friday. View Deal

✅Recommended if: You're not the biggest audiophile and want a device that can fill a room with punchy sound at an affordable price. If you're interested in taking advantage of Alexa+ smarts but don't feel up for upgrading to the latest models, the 5th-gen Echo Dot supports this, but newer models may get updates a lot sooner.

❌Skip this deal if: You want a device that has more than just Matter support. If you have other smart home devices running on Thread or Zigbee, the 5th-gen Echo Dot won't be able to tie them together due to the lack of support. If you have the extra money to spend on the Echo Dot Max, you might as well cash in and make the most of its upgraded capabilities.

Echo Dot Max: was $199.99 now $49.99
One of Amazon's newest smart speakers on the scene is less than $50, and it's a beast. With a two-way speaker system, its audio performance is a significant upgrade compared to its predecessor and is one of the first flagship Alexa+ speakers — meaning it comes with the AI-powered assistant's smarts out of the box. View Deal

✅Recommended if: You've been using a previous-gen smart speaker for a few years and want a bit of an audio boost. Compared to the 5th-gen Echo Dot, it delivers three times the bass, which can be credited to its revamped audio smarts — packing a two-way system with a dedicated subwoofer and tweeter.

If your old smart home hub is giving you nothing but laggy responses, this is your next reason to upgrade. The Echo Dot Max is powered by the AZ3 chip to help Alexa respond to your requests with more speed and accuracy, as well as better wake-word detection and on-device processing for AI tasks.

It's also Matter, Thread, and Zigbee compatible, so if you have other devices dotted around in your setup, the Echo Dot Max can fit in smoothly as a new central hub.

❌Skip this deal if: You're satisfied with the current audio performance and responsiveness of your current smart speaker. The Echo Dot Max is recommended for those who can tell the difference in audio quality and want the upgrade; if this isn't a huge concern for you and you need a device that just gets the job done, previous-gen models are still solid alternatives.

item.title: Galaxy S27 Ultra leak reveals Samsung is stripping away another camera feature
item.dc:content:
Samsung might be gearing up for another big change to its flagship phone cameras. A new leak suggests Samsung is likely to ditch the laser autofocus hardware, possibly taking the 3x telephoto camera with it. That’s two changes to the rear camera system, and while neither is necessarily a recipe for photographic trouble, it does bring up an interesting question: what does Samsung intend to use instead?

The claim comes from well-known leaker Ice Universe, who shared the alleged changes on X. Samsung has been using laser autofocus in its Ultra phones since the Galaxy S21 Ultra, so this is a departure from a camera setup the company has used for several generations.

For the uninitiated, the laser autofocus module is supposed to emit an infrared beam and calculate the time it takes to bounce back from a subject, then use the distance information to assist the camera in locking focus.

This is particularly helpful in low-light situations, where traditional phase-detection autofocus (PDAF) can struggle. But laser autofocus has its own limitations. It struggles with distant subjects, bright sunlight and moving objects.

That doesn't necessarily mean the S27 Ultra will have a worse camera. Autofocus technology has come a long way. Both dual-pixel and all-pixel autofocus can calculate the distance to a subject by using multiple light-sensitive areas across the image sensor. This technology is already being used in some of Samsung’s other flagship devices, so the ditching of a separate laser module is not necessarily a step backward.

A bigger camera overhaul could be coming

It’s also rumored that Samsung might utilize its new 200MP ISOCELL HP6 sensor for the Galaxy S27 Ultra and S27 Pro. Previous reports have indicated support for LOFIC, a technology that’s designed to improve HDR photography and preserve detail in the brightest and darkest parts of a photo. It’s not known if the new sensor will also introduce an advanced autofocus system as well.

The bigger question is what these hardware changes portend for everyday photography. The lack of a dedicated 3x camera may mean more reliance on cropping the sensor for zoom ranges in between. The removal of laser autofocus may mean more reliance on the main sensor’s focusing system.

None of these changes have been confirmed by Samsung, and we won’t see the Galaxy S27 family until the first quarter of 2027. Whether these rumored changes are a smart play for newer imaging tech or just another instance of stripping out useful hardware to cut costs is something buyers will want answered before splashing out flagship money.

item.title: Google Gemini AI gets a token saving update that anyone can appreciate — and better native file support
item.dc:content:
What you need to know

  • Google Gemini has a new ‘File Slicing Controls’ feature that lets you target specific elements of a file for analysis, saving you tokens
  • Works across Gemini and Google AI Studio, meaning it’ll work with not just docs and spreadsheets, but audio and video files too
  • The update also introduces better handling of Microsoft Office and OpenDocument file formats

If you’ve ever come up against a usage limit when sending your Gemini AI assistants off to get a job done, a new capability for Google’s artificial intelligence platform could save you the hassle — and a bunch of time in the process.

The company has just announced a new ‘File Slicing Controls’ feature, rolling out across all its models. In a nutshell, it lets you specify which elements of a file you want Gemini to focus on before it gets to work, rather than having the model do a deep scan of an entire file up front, saving you costly usage tokens in the process.

Though it’s primarily aimed at developers, there are elements here anyone can benefit from. The ‘Skim Then Zoom’ workflow is particularly useful — you can, for instance, tell the AI to summarise and explain just the text of a select range of pages in a PDF, and it’ll skim over the other pages and any associated images, just focussing on the passages you request, clawing back time and tokens.

  • 25+ Black Friday Deals for Android lovers: From glorious Galaxy to Pixel perfection

5 ways File Slicing Controls will save you Gemini headaches

Breaking it down, this might prove one of the most intuitively-useful updates to Gemini in a while:

  1. You no longer have to pre-chop your files: If you were trying to save tokens previously, you may have had to resort to creating a separate version of a file — a reduced page count PDF, a single table spreadsheet, or a shortened video clip — to get the AI to focus its attention on one area without wasting tokens on the contextual scan of the rest.
  2. Greater agent autonomy: Gemini now better understands how to focus in on select layers of information in a file — you don’t have to babysit the specific guardrails of the agent any more, and can have greater faith in its ability to hone in on what you want it to.
  3. Targeted info = fewer hallucinations: By giving the agent just a select window of information to work with, it’s less likely to hallucinate by drawing on potentially unwanted information elsewhere in a video, file or document.
  4. Fewer “Context Limit” errors, and fewer tokens needed: This is a big win — if you’re regularly hitting file size limits or ‘conversation too long’ style errors when using Gemini, that’s usually because you’ve hit the end of your token allowance (the amount of tasks / data an agent can ingest do before you’ve got to cough up more moolah). By specifying the precise chunks you want analysed, you’re saving on that allowance and won’t hit those errors so quickly or so often.
  5. Better native file format support: This bit is tucked away in the announcement, but the update also improves Gemini’s handling of Microsoft Office file formats, such as those created in Word, Excel and Powerpoint, and OpenDocument files. It can read them in their native form, meaning they won’t have to be converted by Gemini (or you) before the agent can tackle them, saving you tokens (or time) in the process.

For the full run through of how the feature works, check out the Google Blog.

item.title: Forget the iPad mini: This powerful compact Android tablet is now $300 off
item.dc:content:
If you've been looking for a compact Android tablet that can compete with Apple's iPad mini, the Lenovo Legion Tab Gen 5 is arguably one of the best options out there. While the tablet is a little expensive at its usual $900 price, Lenovo's flagship gaming tablet is now down to just $600, saving you a massive $300 (33%).

The Lenovo Legion Tab Gen 5 packs flagship-level performance into a compact tablet with an 8.8-inch 165Hz display, Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chipset, 12GB of RAM, 256GB of storage, and a massive 9,000mAh battery. It's now $300 off ahead of Black Friday.View Deal

  • Browse all the latest Black Friday Amazon deals

✅Recommended if: You want a compact Android tablet with flagship performance, a high refresh rate display, and excellent battery capacity for gaming, watching movies, or traveling.

❌Skip this deal if: You prefer a larger screen for productivity, specifically want an OLED display, or only need a basic tablet for browsing and streaming.

One of my favorite things about the Lenovo Legion Tab Gen 5 is its form factor. There aren't many compact Android tablets on the market that offer flagship-level specs, but the Legion Tab Gen 5 manages to pack some pretty powerful hardware into a device with an 8.8-inch display.

And while it uses an IPS LCD panel rather than an AMOLED display, it supports a refresh rate of up to 165Hz, which is considerably higher than the 60Hz display you get on the iPad mini.

But the biggest reason to consider the Legion Tab Gen 5 is its performance. The tablet is powered by Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chipset, paired with 12GB of RAM and 256GB of onboard storage. Even though it's no longer Qualcomm's latest flagship chipset, it's still one of the most powerful processors you'll find in an Android tablet.

Lenovo has also managed to pack a massive 9,000mAh battery into this compact tablet, which should give you plenty of gaming time without having to constantly reach for a charger.

And even if you're not particularly into gaming, I think the Legion Tab Gen 5 makes for a pretty great travel companion. Its 8.8-inch display is big enough to comfortably watch movies, read books, or browse the web on a long flight, but the tablet itself is still compact enough to carry around without taking up much space in your backpack.

On the whole, if you've been waiting for a proper Android alternative to the iPad mini that doesn't compromise on performance, the Lenovo Legion Tab Gen 5 is definitely worth checking out. Its usual $900 price makes it a little difficult to recommend, but at $600, it's a much more compelling option.

item.title: Samsung looks to Apple’s Dynamic Island for a potential Now Bar redesign — and it’s been a long time coming
item.dc:content:
What you need to know

  • A new leak reveals a possible redesign for Samsung's Now Bar, which could move front-and-center like Apple's Dynamic Island
  • Samsung could also roll out 'Moments effects', a downloadable animations function for Now Bar
  • Both are projected to launch with the Galaxy S27 Series, but the tech company hasn't issued an official announcement yet

For years, Apple has taken pages out of Samsung's book when developing its own devices — just look at the iPhone Duo, which arrived seven years after Samsung's first foldable. But oh, how the tables have turned.

Samsung is busy preparing for its next smartphone lineup, the Galaxy S27 Series, and a new leak points to a possible redesign for the Live Notifications view in the Now Bar, which could be moving front and center where the front camera sits. SamMobile spotted the changes while sifting through the One UI 9.5 software.

As it stands, the Now Bar (which displays real-time tools such as timers, map directions, and other ongoing activities) sits in the top-left corner next to the time display. If it looks familiar to you, you're not alone — numerous users have compared it to Apple's flagship Dynamic Island feature, which was introduced with the iPhone 14 Pro back in 2022.

While the Now Bar is projected for a redesign, its lock screen version is set to remain in its usual position at the bottom-center of the smartphone display.

However, it's not just the design that Samsung is drawing inspiration from Apple. Instead of the current up-and-down swipe navigation you use to view your Live Notifications, the leak reveals a new left-to-right swipe function when flicking through your ongoing activities in its new pill-shaped form, just like the Dynamic Island.

But where Samsung could take it a step further is with a new Now Bar settings page, which was also spotted in the leaked firmware. As well as the redesign, SamMobile also found 'Moments effects', a new page within the Now Bar where you can download add-on packs that show basic animations.

Right now, only the 'Sports' pack is listed as an available add-on, which displays the prompt "Celebrate your favourite teams’ scores and wins. Available for select sports supported by Google Sports". When a team you're tracking via Google Sports scores or wins, it triggers a fun animation that appears in the Now Bar. Though this feature was softly introduced in the One UI 9.5 Beta 1, the leak suggests Samsung has plans to add more categories in the future.

These at-a-glance notification centers are pretty much the new norm with every smartphone release. Though Apple arguably pioneered it a few years ago, countless tech brands have followed suit with their own versions, so it was only a matter of time before Samsung had to bite the bullet.

There's no doubt the Now Bar redesign will be a welcome quality-of-life upgrade, but we won't know anything for certain until Samsung decides when it's the right time to divulge more information.

item.title: This brand is bringing the most surprising Android trend of 2026 to a budget smartphone
item.dc:content:
What you need to know

  • Smartphone maker Doogee has announced a new wide-screen phone
  • The Wide Core runs on the entry-level Unisoc T750 chipset, with RAM and storage starting at 3GB+64GB
  • These specs suggest that it will be more affordable than other wide-screen options and possibly come in at under $400

It looks like wide-screen phones are the new big Android phone trend of 2026, with the popularity of the passport-style foldable Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 and the arrival of more recent, non-folding contenders like Huawei's new OSTA O1 Pro.

Now, rugged smartphone brand Doogee is bringing the form factor to a more affordable market segment with its new Wide Core model. It looks quite similar to the existing, more premium Huawei Pura X View, with a similar maroon color option and visor-like camera island design.

item.title: Amazon knocks more than $200 off the Google Pixel 10 in its Black Friday sale
item.dc:content:
Editor's note - This article's headline previously claimed that this ongoing discount represented a new lowest-ever price for the Google Pixel 10. That is not the case, as the handset was previously discounted to $534 in June 2026, and the article has been updated to reflect this.

Black Friday is the best time to upgrade your flagship smartphone without breaking the bank, as prices keep going up. Google’s regular flagship has to be a contender if you want a small Android phone with good cameras and useful software.

Right now, the unlocked Google Pixel 10 is on sale at Amazon for $593, down from its usual price of $799. That's 26% off, saving you over $200 and tying the lowest price we've seen for this model since mid-July. You’ll want to act fast, though, as this deal is live only while supplies last.

The Pixel 10 combines Google's software experience with practical AI features, a versatile triple-camera system, and a bright OLED display. At under $599, you're getting a phone that originally launched at $799 for considerably less.View Deal

✅ Recommended if: You’re an average smartphone user, an iPhone switcher or a budget buyer who likes clean software, useful AI features and a simple design.

❌ Skip this deal if: You’re a heavy mobile gamer, a videographer, a power user who hates slow charging, or you own a recent Pixel already.

The Pixel 10 isn't trying too hard to be different, with a 6.3-inch screen and a design that's pretty much "business as usual." The software experience is clean and a big part of the appeal, especially if you prefer Google's take on Android over heavily customized interfaces. It's also worth considering if you're thinking of moving away from an iPhone.

One of the phone’s big selling points is its triple rear-camera setup, which adds a 5x telephoto lens with up to 20x Super Res Zoom. You also get Google’s Tensor G5 processor and 12GB of RAM, along with software features meant to make everyday tasks more convenient. That said, the Tensor G5 isn't particularly powerful for demanding workloads, so heavy gamers may want to look elsewhere.

The numbers make the device a more interesting deal. It has a 6.3-inch Actua OLED panel with a 120Hz refresh rate and peak brightness of up to 3,000 nits. Google claims you’ll get over 24 hours of battery life, and the Qi2 Pixelsnap magnetic wireless charger is yet another handy convenience. The phone is also IP68 water and dust resistant and has Corning Gorilla Glass Victus 2 protection.

Of course, $599 doesn’t mean the Pixel 10 is without compromises. You get downgraded main and ultrawide camera sensors, slow charging speeds and buggy software updates that can make the experience frustrating. If raw performance, fast charging or heavy-duty video work are what you are after, the Pixel 10 isn't the phone we'd recommend.

item.title: Why spend $1,400 on the Galaxy S26 Ultra? This Samsung flagship is down to just $684
item.dc:content:
Samsung may have already launched the Galaxy S26 series, but you don't necessarily need to buy one of its latest smartphones to get a flagship experience.

In fact, one of Samsung's most underrated smartphones from last year, the Galaxy S25 Plus, is now down to just $684, a massive 32% discount from its usual $1,000 price. And at this price, it's the only Samsung phone I'd buy this Black Friday.

The Samsung Galaxy S25 Plus offers much of what you'd expect from a flagship smartphone, including a 6.7-inch 120Hz AMOLED display, Snapdragon 8 Elite chipset, 12GB of RAM, 256GB of storage, and a sizable 4,900mAh battery. It's now available for just $684, saving you $316 ahead of Black Friday.View Deal

  • Browse all the latest Black Friday Amazon deals

✅Recommended if: You want a big-screen Samsung flagship with excellent performance, solid battery life, versatile cameras, and years of software support without spending $1,000.

❌Skip this deal if: You prefer compact smartphones, want the S Pen and more advanced zoom cameras of the Ultra model, or need the absolute latest hardware.

The Galaxy S25 Plus often gets overlooked in Samsung's flagship lineup, largely because most people either go for the more affordable base model or spend a little extra to get the Ultra. But the Galaxy S25 Plus strikes a pretty good balance between the two, especially at its discounted price.

For starters, you get a big 6.7-inch Dynamic AMOLED 2X display with an adaptive 120Hz refresh rate. Samsung arguably makes some of the best smartphone displays on the market, and the Galaxy S25 Plus is no exception. The phone has also already been updated to Android 17 with One UI 9, so you're getting much of the same software experience as Samsung's newer flagships.

And while the Galaxy S25 Plus may no longer feature Qualcomm's latest chipset, the Snapdragon 8 Elite is still a very capable processor, even in 2026. Paired with 12GB of RAM and 256GB of onboard storage, the phone should have no trouble handling pretty much anything you throw at it.

You're also getting a pretty versatile camera setup on the back. The Galaxy S25 Plus features a 50MP primary camera, a 10MP telephoto camera with 3x optical zoom, and a 12MP ultrawide sensor. Sure, you're missing out on some of the more advanced camera hardware of the Ultra model, but for most people, this setup should be more than enough.

One of the best things about the Galaxy S25 Plus is its sizable 4,900mAh battery, which is still among the largest you'll find on a Samsung phone. It also supports the same 45W wired charging as the Galaxy S25 Ultra, along with 15W Qi2-ready wireless charging with a compatible magnetic case.

item.title: Black Friday knocked 25% off Nothing Phone 3—price is so good, it's already in my cart
item.dc:content:
There's a conversation to be had about the Nothing Phone 3. This phone is the company's "flagship." It's an exciting phone with a few noteworthy changes, but we'll get into the details in a moment.

The Nothing Phone 3 has dropped 29% on Amazon for Black Friday, and it's at a price that's got it in my cart already.

The Phone 3 is Nothing's flagship. It's a phone that has upgraded its camera/video capabilities over previous generations. The Phone 3 also includes a new LED dot matrix that changes our perception of the old Glyph lighting.View Deal

There are deals on this phone all over (you can find a few more down below). However, if you prefer, Nothing's U.S. storefront is running a Black Friday sale. There's one week left. You can find the Phone 3 at the price listed above on its U.S. store.

The Nothing Phone 3 is ✅ recommended if you're looking for a fabulous phone. You might think I'm joking, but that's the reality. Nothing revamped the Phone 3's design, adding a dot-matrix panel on the back. If you love taking pictures or recording videos, the Phone 3 is definitely a keeper. Compared to the other devices in the series, the Phone 3's cameras have definitely taken a step forward. You'll also find a 5,150mAh battery, a 6.6-inch display, a triple 50MP camera array, and more.

Now, you can ❌ skip this deal if you need a phone that's actually a flagship. It's probably one of our greatest gripes with the Nothing Phone 3. The device, while the brand categorizes it as a "flagship," misses the mark. It features Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8s Gen 4, a mid-range chip with "accessible premium features." But it still doesn't carry the power you'd expect from a true flagship chip, like the Snapdragon 8 Elite.

We were hoping for a new Nothing flagship this year—in 2026—but the company said otherwise. In January, Nothing's CEO, Carl Pei, said the Phone 3 would be the brand's 2026 flagship. There were no plans to unveil another, as it moved ahead with the Phone 4a series. What's more, Nothing committed to introducing new features for the Phone 3 through Nothing OS 4 updates.

This wasn't necessarily a bad thing. The Phone 3 captured consumers when it launched. The LED dot matrix was a new take on the Glyph Lightning we were used to, and its vibrant OLED screen was a welcome addition. Its design shake-up also keeps up those unmistakable Nothing vibes. However, the main thing is that the phone isn't truly a flagship. Its chip of choice and GPU could be better. The Phone 3 falls within a mid-range sector if you focus on that alone.

It's also another reason this Black Friday deal is so good. At its actual starting price, we can't justify the device. However, with this sweet price drop, it's worth it given the software, camera and video upgrades, display, long battery life, and fast charging.

item.title: This Nothing Ear 3 Black Friday deal has us losing our minds—the audio is good, but the price drop is better
item.dc:content:
For a pair of third-generation earbuds, you'd imagine (or at least hope for) major upgrades. Nothing delivered in a few areas where we were looking for improvements. What's more, the Nothing Ear 3 introduces a new way to interact with the device and its case.

Before we get too ahead of ourselves, there's a pair of Black Friday deals for the Nothing Ear 3 that drop them by almost 40%.

The Nothing Ear 3 continues the classic Nothing transparent design with longer battery life, redesigned audio drivers, and support for LDAC hi-res audio. The Ear 3 introduced an aluminum case with a dual-microphone system.View Deal

If you prefer, you can also find these deals on Nothing's U.S. website during its Black Friday sale.

These earbuds are ✅ recommended if you value a device that won't drop out on you. The Nothing Ear 3 battery life is a major highlight. Compared to the Ear 1 and Ear 2, the Ear 3 delivers roughly 5.5 hours of listening time per bud (Adaptive ANC enabled). This jumps to 10 hours if you disable ANC, which just means more tunes or podcasts or shows/movies. Another interesting feature with the Ear 3 is Super Mic. It is a dual-microphone system in the charging case. Pressing the TALK button switches audio from your earbuds to your case—more on this in a moment.

However, you should probably ❌ skip this deal if you need earbuds with more reliable ANC/transparency modes. The Ear 3 falls kind of flat in these areas, leaving you wanting more. What's more, while we've praised the upgraded battery life, the Ear 3 isn't for you if you want great audio and long battery life. That sounds like a no-brainer, right? If you want LDAC audio and ANC, your battery life drops to ~3.5 hours per bud.

Super Mic is the big new thing for the Nothing Ear 3. Press the TALK button to switch your audio output to the case. This is intended for users on calls or taking a voice memo. One thing that we noted in our review is that the Ear 3 flips the switch on a classic sentiment. Wireless earbuds aren't renowned for "great" mics. However, with the dual microphone system in the case, it offers something with more substance.

The redesigned 12mm drivers are also a high point for the Ear 3. Factor in its LDAC audio support and you've got a pair of buds that are pretty handy. What's more, its original starting price wasn't terrible compared to the competition. Since it's Black Friday, that price is even more attractive if you're looking for a new pair.

I use a pair of Status Pro X earbuds almost every day, as they're the best-sounding wireless model that I've ever owned. Right now, they can be the best earbuds you've ever heard, too, for an Amazon lowest-ever price of $179 (down from $249) thanks to a new Black Friday deal.

It's all wrapped up in a classy design and comes with a robust companion app that lets you create your own EQ or explore a range of presets for the perfect listening experience.

  • Browse all the latest Black Friday Amazon deals

This is a new lowest-ever price for the Status Pro X buds. Designed for audiophiles, these wireless earbuds offer 24 bit / 96kHz Hi-Res sound with support for the LDAC codec and a superb companion app. They're not cheap, but you can hear every cent.View Deal

✅Recommended if: You want wireless earbuds that simply sound fantastic. The Status Pro X buds deliver crystal-clear, accurate sound with bass that's strong but never overpowering. They support a range of popular codecs, including the high-fidelity LDAC.

There are some disadvantages compared to competitors, which I'll outline in just a moment, but the sound is second to none.

❌Skip this deal if: You want the best noise-cancelling or battery life. I've tested plenty of wireless earbuds, and while none can beat the Status Pro X for sound, there are plenty of other options that offer better ANC and battery life.

For a record-low price, you can get the Echo Show 8 smart display for $99.99 down from $199.99, a generous $ 100 off. But what does a smart display do that a smart speaker can't?

Firstly, the Echo Show 8 is a hybrid between the two, offering robust audio and voice command features you get with a smart speaker, while giving you all the visual and touchscreen components you get with a tablet. item.title: Five expert tips for getting the best Android phone deals this Black Friday
item.dc:content:
Black Friday 2027 is almost here, and Android phone deals are already coming in fast. If you're trying to upgrade your mobile, then the year's biggest sales event is the perfect chance to secure a bargain – but it's not without its risks.

You want to make sure that you're getting the very best value for your money, picking the right device for your needs, and securing a genuine discount that's actually better than the kind of price cuts you might see at other times of the year.

QUICK LINKS TO THE BIG BLACK FRIDAY SALES

  • Amazon: Big savings on tech essentials
  • Best Buy: Half price TVs, laptops, gadgets and more
  • Walmart: Members get early access to giant savings
  • Target: Great for pre-Christmas gifting prep
  • T-Mobile: Free premium handsets — including Samsung Galaxy — with select plans
  • Samsung: Up to $1,000 off 2026 flagship devices
  • Mint Mobile: Half price unlimited data with top Google Pixel devices

I've been covering Black Friday annually for almost half a decade now, so I know how to navigate the deal landscape like the back of my hand and identify what separates a bad deal from an absolute bargain. To that end, here are my five expert tips for buying an Android phone this Black Friday.

1. Aim for more than 4GB of RAM, but swerve RAM Turbo

You might be tempted to fire up Amazon and beeline straight for the most heavily discounted handsets, but there are some key specs to watch that are genuinely worth paying a little more for if you have the budget.

For most users, the phone's chipset isn't going to make a huge difference, as mid-range and even budget models now pack modern enough chips to handle everyday tasks like browsing the web, sending emails, or checking social media smoothly.

I would pay attention to the RAM and storage capacity of the phone above all else. Adequate RAM helps ensure the phone can handle multiple apps, as well as important background tasks, without any slowdown or annoying refreshes.

Consider 4GB the absolute bare minimum for any phone that you're buying in 2026, though more is always better. 6GB is the perfect sweet spot and should help future-proof the device, while 8GB and above can accommodate more complex multitasking and gaming. This will generally come at a premium, though.

Some brands advertise a feature called RAM Plus, Memory Extension, RAM Turbo, or similar, which uses some of the phone's internal storage as additional RAM, rather than a dedicated chip. An easy way to spot this is when a spec sheet lists something like "4GB RAM + 4GB RAM Plus". The extra RAM might look like a nice bonus, but you should be wary of it, as it will take up valuable storage space and, as a rule, does not perform as well as the real deal.

2. You need 128GB of storage at least

Speaking of storage, some manufacturers are still selling phones with just 64GB (or, in extreme cases, even less) of storage space built in. Certain Android skins (like Samsung's OneUI) can take up to 40GB of space out of the box, so you will almost immediately find yourself without enough space for apps, photos, music, movies, and so on.

Even if it's not an issue straight away, low storage space can severely limit the practicality of a phone in the long term too, as it makes it much more difficult to keep the operating system and your apps up to date. Go for at least 128GB to give yourself enough room for everything that you need, as well as any updates.

If you're a hardcore mobile gamer, then 256GB is a more realistic starting point, as modern titles like Neverness to Everness take up almost 30GB of space alone.

Also be on the lookout for phones that support microSD storage expansion. It's become quite a rare feature these days as companies ditch it in favor of thinner chassis designs, but the option to add a microSD card for extra space to store your files can come in handy if you're struggling to free up space down the line.

3. Ask if you really need those flagship features

You can broadly separate the smartphone market into three segments: budget, mid-range, and flagship.

Flagship models are the most expensive options in a brand's lineup, designed for top-of-the-line performance and the most advanced features, while budget options have more modest spec sheets but come at a much more affordable price.

The mid-range sits, well, in the middle of those two, giving you some of the qualities of a flagship without the high asking price.

A good way to save money is to always ask yourself whether you really need to splash out for the flagship offering, or can make do with the mid-range or budget alternatives.

Take the current Samsung Galaxy line as an example. The flagship $1,299+ Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra packs the lightning-fast Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 SoC, boasts a 200MP rear camera, and comes with a built-in stylus as well as an innovative privacy display that stops passersby from being able to snoop on your screen.

This sounds fantastic, but is that really worth almost double the cost of the mid-range Galaxy S26 FE? The S26 FE has a weaker, but still capable, Exynos 2500 chip, a more modest 50MP rear camera, and lacks both the built-in stylus and privacy display.

If you're not a hardcore gamer, the chip isn't going to make much of a difference in day-to-day use, and while the lesser camera might sting the one time a year you're taking holiday snaps, the privacy display and stylus are likely not worth the upgrade unless you're dead set on using both features a lot.

4. Check update support carefully

You wouldn't buy milk that's one day away from its expiration date, and, believe it or not, the same principle applies to phones.

Every phone manufacturer releases documentation detailing how many updates it will provide for a certain model, and finding out that number is imperative before you hit buy.

Be aware that update policies can vary by region. Check local support pages to make sure that the promised number of updates actually applies to you in order to avoid any nasty surprises.

Generally, phone brands will offer two separate figures. One tells you how many Android OS updates a phone will get (introducing new features, etc.), and the other concerns the number of years of security updates. The latter is by far the most important: using a phone without security updates leaves you at increasing risk of falling victim to unpatched security vulnerabilities, so it should be avoided whenever possible.

Try to get as many years of security update support as you can. 1 to 2 years should be avoided unless the phone is very cheap and you're prepared to replace it when it runs out, while 3 to 4 years is common but not ideal. 5, 6, or even 7 years of security updates is perfect and will ensure you remain protected until it's time for your next upgrade.

Always take into account the fact that these figures begin when the phone was released, rather than when you're buying it. If you're purchasing a model that came out three years ago that only has four years of security updates planned, you're getting just one year by the time it's in your hands.

I like to divide the sale price of a phone by the number of years of support remaining to work out just how much it's costing me per year of use, as I find that figure much more helpful than a flat price when it comes to working out how good value it is.

Don't spend hundreds on a phone that's going to be out of date and vulnerable to security exploits in six months!

5. Always check refurbished options

It may sound obvious, but you should weigh up second-hand or refurbished options as well. Sometimes you can save a fortune by picking up a used model that's practically indistinguishable from a new one.

Black Friday 2027 is almost here, and Android phone deals are already coming in fast. If you're trying to upgrade your mobile, then the year's biggest sales event is the perfect chance to secure a bargain – but it's not without its risks.

You want to make sure that you're getting the very best value for your money, picking the right device for your needs, and securing a genuine discount that's actually better than the kind of price cuts you might see at other times of the year.

QUICK LINKS TO THE BIG BLACK FRIDAY SALES

  • Amazon: Big savings on tech essentials
  • Best Buy: Half price TVs, laptops, gadgets and more
  • Walmart: Members get early access to giant savings
  • Target: Great for pre-Christmas gifting prep
  • T-Mobile: Free premium handsets — including Samsung Galaxy — with select plans
  • Samsung: Up to $1,000 off 2026 flagship devices
  • Mint Mobile: Half price unlimited data with top Google Pixel devices

I've been covering Black Friday annually for almost half a decade now, so I know how to navigate the deal landscape like the back of my hand and identify what separates a bad deal from an absolute bargain. To that end, here are my five expert tips for buying an Android phone this Black Friday.

1. Aim for more than 4GB of RAM, but swerve RAM Turbo

You might be tempted to fire up Amazon and beeline straight for the most heavily discounted handsets, but there are some key specs to watch that are genuinely worth paying a little more for if you have the budget.

For most users, the phone's chipset isn't going to make a huge difference, as mid-range and even budget models now pack modern enough chips to handle everyday tasks like browsing the web, sending emails, or checking social media smoothly.

I would pay attention to the RAM and storage capacity of the phone above all else. Adequate RAM helps ensure the phone can handle multiple apps, as well as important background tasks, without any slowdown or annoying refreshes.

Consider 4GB the absolute bare minimum for any phone that you're buying in 2026, though more is always better. 6GB is the perfect sweet spot and should help future-proof the device, while 8GB and above can accommodate more complex multitasking and gaming. This will generally come at a premium, though.

Some brands advertise a feature called RAM Plus, Memory Extension, RAM Turbo, or similar, which uses some of the phone's internal storage as additional RAM, rather than a dedicated chip. An easy way to spot this is when a spec sheet lists something like "4GB RAM + 4GB RAM Plus". The extra RAM might look like a nice bonus, but you should be wary of it, as it will take up valuable storage space and, as a rule, does not perform as well as the real deal.

2. You need 128GB of storage at least

Speaking of storage, some manufacturers are still selling phones with just 64GB (or, in extreme cases, even less) of storage space built in. Certain Android skins (like Samsung's OneUI) can take up to 40GB of space out of the box, so you will almost immediately find yourself without enough space for apps, photos, music, movies, and so on.

Even if it's not an issue straight away, low storage space can severely limit the practicality of a phone in the long term too, as it makes it much more difficult to keep the operating system and your apps up to date. Go for at least 128GB to give yourself enough room for everything that you need, as well as any updates.

If you're a hardcore mobile gamer, then 256GB is a more realistic starting point, as modern titles like Neverness to Everness take up almost 30GB of space alone.

Also be on the lookout for phones that support microSD storage expansion. It's become quite a rare feature these days as companies ditch it in favor of thinner chassis designs, but the option to add a microSD card for extra space to store your files can come in handy if you're struggling to free up space down the line.

3. Ask if you really need those flagship features

You can broadly separate the smartphone market into three segments: budget, mid-range, and flagship.

Flagship models are the most expensive options in a brand's lineup, designed for top-of-the-line performance and the most advanced features, while budget options have more modest spec sheets but come at a much more affordable price.

The mid-range sits, well, in the middle of those two, giving you some of the qualities of a flagship without the high asking price.

A good way to save money is to always ask yourself whether you really need to splash out for the flagship offering, or can make do with the mid-range or budget alternatives.

Take the current Samsung Galaxy line as an example. The flagship $1,299+ Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra packs the lightning-fast Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 SoC, boasts a 200MP rear camera, and comes with a built-in stylus as well as an innovative privacy display that stops passersby from being able to snoop on your screen.

This sounds fantastic, but is that really worth almost double the cost of the mid-range Galaxy S26 FE? The S26 FE has a weaker, but still capable, Exynos 2500 chip, a more modest 50MP rear camera, and lacks both the built-in stylus and privacy display.

If you're not a hardcore gamer, the chip isn't going to make much of a difference in day-to-day use, and while the lesser camera might sting the one time a year you're taking holiday snaps, the privacy display and stylus are likely not worth the upgrade unless you're dead set on using both features a lot.

4. Check update support carefully

You wouldn't buy milk that's one day away from its expiration date, and, believe it or not, the same principle applies to phones.

Every phone manufacturer releases documentation detailing how many updates it will provide for a certain model, and finding out that number is imperative before you hit buy.

Be aware that update policies can vary by region. Check local support pages to make sure that the promised number of updates actually applies to you in order to avoid any nasty surprises.

Generally, phone brands will offer two separate figures. One tells you how many Android OS updates a phone will get (introducing new features, etc.), and the other concerns the number of years of security updates. The latter is by far the most important: using a phone without security updates leaves you at increasing risk of falling victim to unpatched security vulnerabilities, so it should be avoided whenever possible.

Try to get as many years of security update support as you can. 1 to 2 years should be avoided unless the phone is very cheap and you're prepared to replace it when it runs out, while 3 to 4 years is common but not ideal. 5, 6, or even 7 years of security updates is perfect and will ensure you remain protected until it's time for your next upgrade.

Always take into account the fact that these figures begin when the phone was released, rather than when you're buying it. If you're purchasing a model that came out three years ago that only has four years of security updates planned, you're getting just one year by the time it's in your hands.

I like to divide the sale price of a phone by the number of years of support remaining to work out just how much it's costing me per year of use, as I find that figure much more helpful than a flat price when it comes to working out how good value it is.

item.title: Commodore teams with FiiO for retro wired in-ear headphones that will take you back to 2006… via 1986
item.dc:content:
What you need to know

  • Commodore unveiled its new Talkback Professional In-Ear Monitors
  • The company worked with Fiio to tune its audio for a crisp and detailed output
  • The earbuds are available to pre-order now for $50 / £38.05, but an official release date has yet to be announced

Wired earphones never died, they were simply overshadowed — at least that's what the team at retro-revival tech company Commodore say.

Hot on the heels of its Callback 8020 flip phone, Commodore has stepped back into the world of audio with its new Talkback Professional In-Ear Monitors, which the company describes as another step in its goal to herald 'the return of intentional technology'. Their price tag is also more-than-reasonable at just ($50 / £38.05).

Just like its anti-doomscrolling and de-Googled mobile device, Commodore's new wired earbuds embrace everything we loved about tech from the '00s, with a touch of nostalgia for anyone that remembers Commodore in its 1980s computing heyday. Even its release campaign screams 'frutiger metro'. If you're unfamiliar with the term, just think about classic iTunes ad campaigns from 2006.

Sporting a timeless transparent look, Commodore's Talkback IEMs pack a 3.5mm audio jack and silicon-cushioned earbuds that hook over your ears for added support. There's nothing worse than wearing a pair of the best wireless earbuds, only to have them slip out while you're commuting, working out, or just enjoying some downtime.

Taking inspiration from the past, the earbuds come fitted with an in-line microphone, volume and play/ pause buttons, taking the chore out of reaching for your phone to control every aspect of the playback experience.

But beyond its nostalgic aesthetics, Commodore is looking to provide a bold listening experience at that modest price point.

Partnering with engineers from the audio behemoth Fiio, Commodore wants to ensure that audio isn't compromised, designing its wired IEMs for 'for both casual users and keen audiophiles alike'. According to Commodore, its wired earbuds are fine-tuned to offer clarity and detailed audio, all paired with controlled bass and a balanced mid-range to really enhance its immersive audio capabilities.

Although Bluetooth earbuds can also offer crisp audio along with the convenience of a wireless experience, wired audio accessories tend to be favored more for getting the most of out of your hi-res/ lossless music streaming. They significantly reduce latency (useful when gaming or keeping an eye on lip-sync issues in videos), and direct wired connectivity reduces Bluetooth compression, allowing you to listen to audio close to how it was initially uploaded.

The Commodore Talkback Professional In-Ear Monitors are available to pre-order now, but the company hasn't disclosed an official release date yet.

item.title: Samsung may skip the Galaxy Watch 10 in 2027 as costs pile up
item.dc:content:
Samsung could be skipping its annual smartwatch launches, and the Galaxy Watch 10 could be the first casualty.

According to a fresh report from Korea’s ETNews, the company is considering a two-year release cycle, which means that buyers may need to wait until 2028 for its next major smartwatch upgrade.

The report said Samsung is rethinking its hardware release strategy as mounting manufacturing costs weigh on its mobile business. The mobile unit has posted losses for two quarters in a row, making it harder to justify the costly annual product launches.

The reported change would bring to an end a nine-year tradition dating back to the original Galaxy Watch in 2018. If Samsung follows through on its plan, the Galaxy Watch 9 and the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2, both scheduled for 2026, could be its last flagship wearables until 2027.

Higher prices aren't helping Samsung's smartwatch business

The Galaxy Watch 9 reportedly struggled to meet sales expectations after Samsung increased its price compared with the Galaxy Watch 8. That’s not surprising, given that buyers aren’t seeing enough meaningful improvements to justify paying more for another annual upgrade.

Stretching the release cycle could allow Samsung to reduce research, development, and marketing costs while allowing its engineers to spend more time working on substantial hardware improvements.

Existing Galaxy Watches could get more attention

Releasing a new smartwatch is not a guaranty that Samsung will leave customers waiting for improvements. The company is reportedly planning to focus on software updates and new health features for existing Galaxy Watch models throughout 2027. A cheaper Galaxy Fit fitness band might also help keep its wearable line moving.

The move is said to be part of a wider cost-cutting effort at Samsung. The company is also reportedly looking at cutting production of its Galaxy A smartphones by about 20% and shifting focus to its higher-margin Galaxy S27 Pro and Ultra devices.

Samsung has not officially confirmed the reported changes. But fewer launches a year might be a good thing for consumers if the company takes that time to offer upgrades worth paying for. What really matters is whether Samsung can improve its current watches without sacrificing long-term software support as yet another casualty of its cost-cutting plans.

item.title: The Xiaomi 18 Pro's back display is its killer feature — and I hope it comes to more Android phones
item.dc:content:
This is a big year for Xiaomi as the new Xiaomi 18 Pro and Xiaomi 18 Pro Max are launching globally. I've been using them for a week, and normally I’d quickly settle on it being “an excellent flagship smartphone that's super capable, but doesn't excite me as much as a folding phone."

Except, the Xiaomi 18 Pro has a serious secret weapon: an innovative back display.

It's not the first Xiaomi Pro phone with a rear display, but it is the first to come out globally, and it was worth the wait. I'm absolutely blown away, it's so good, Google should make it a key part of Android.

Here's what it can do, why it's so good, and the feature that shows the future of Android smartphones.

A new take on a second screen

Xiaomi isn't the first to experiment with second screens. Android has long had attempts to add extra screens, side edges for notifications, or Glyph displays/notification lights to tell you something.

Yet all of these felt like gimmicks. The closest we've come to a genuinely usable second screen is the Moto Razr, and that's because it's a folding phone and the cover display is just a small phone screen. None of them were inherently useful and even if they were at first, they quickly lost their utility.

It turns out that there's a good reason for that. The onus is generally on the company to provide an infinite number of options and use cases, and then predict what else you might like.

Then there's the added problem of persuading developers to update their apps to use this real estate or, more likely, to create new apps for it. Since the second iPhone, it's been clear that apps and experiences matter a lot for feature adoption, and a secondary display is no exception.

It turns out there's a great answer to all of these problems: AI. That's the magic that makes this second screen inherently useful – giving you something you'll actually use multiple times a day.

Gemini is the secret weapon that changes everything

Have you heard of vibe coding? It’s a term used to describe building apps and software with vibes, aka describing changes and having AI make them, rather than coding the changes yourself. I’ve been using it all year to build several platforms and apps, and it’s revolutionary. You can type simple sentences, and AI will make the changes.

Google and Xiaomi have taken this concept further with a new feature called GenAI apps. As the name suggests, it stands for Generative AI apps, or using AI to generate entire apps with one message. This is the secret to making the secondary display more useful: instead of relying on a company to build everything you need, you can build it yourself.

We’ve all been there: you’re stuck in the doctor’s waiting room, lying in bed, or otherwise just looking for something to do. Sure, you can play yet another game, or you can have some fun and create new things to try on the back display. It takes three to five minutes to build a polished, optimized app specifically for the back display.

Simply put: GenAI apps are magnificent, and a glimpse of how we’ll use our phones in the future.

The Xiaomi 18 Pro makes regular phones as exciting as a folding phone

Think about how useful this is: playing DnD and you’ve lost the dice? Create new dice in just a minute on your phone. Want to pin your shopping list for when you go shopping? Easy. Love flipping coins? There’s an app for that. I created one in 3 minutes; it’s that easy – and the GenAI app's chat window had it as one of the suggested apps.

It’s not just about creating your own apps: Xiaomi has built a series of useful, fun, or interactive apps that are easy to use, from an activity and workout tracker to a ninja swipe game, and many more in between. The only real downside? You can install a maximum of 12 at a time, but it is super easy to install or remove them in just a few seconds.

The back display does more than just show apps

Since Xiaomi first built the rear display, I’ve been waiting for them to give this a wow factor that makes it a necessity. GenAI apps offer that wow factor, since you can build whatever you want in just a few minutes. Yes, there are monthly limits on how many apps you can create, but nonetheless, I can’t stop using the Xiaomi 18 Pro back display.

As you might expect, there’s one further added benefit: it’s the perfect viewfinder for selfies. The back display solves the selfie problem: front cameras are usually lower quality than rear cameras, and rear cameras usually don't let you see what you are capturing (unless you're using a foldable).

The Xiaomi 18 Pro rear display lets you use the full camera UX, including capturing in portrait or landscape based on the phone's orientation when you’re capturing. It’s essentially the same as using the main display, and surprisingly useful for selfies, especially as you can use gestures like holding your palm up to capture the photo.

Beyond that, Xiaomi added built-in support for Google Maps, Spotify, and YouTube Music on the rear screen – letting you glance at turn-by-turn directions or control playback without waking the main display – alongside widgets, panels, and a range of wallpaper and clock styles.

One of my favorites lets you display different inspirational quotes, and considering how positive affirmations can be for your mental health, it’s a great face to have. There’s also a customizable Always On Display for glancing at pinned notes, widgets, or the time while your phone sits face-down.

Dear Google, make this a thing!

I’m so enamored with the Xiaomi 18 Pro and its rear screen that there’s only one thing I want: for Google to make this the default in Android. Every Android phone maker should adopt this; Google should add full support in the core OS, and the Play Store should include a classifier for back-display apps.

This would solve the other key problem: you can build apps, but you can’t share them with anyone else. A future marketplace or way to surface apps other people have built would build momentum and also let people sell, earn, and do more. Considering how themes are often sold for a low price and theme stores are incredibly popular, I can see how this would be a win for all users.

In the meantime, I’m off to build some more Gen AI apps. The only thing limiting me? Deciding what to build next.
item.description: Dear Google, all I want for Christmas is the Xiaomi 18 Pro back display on every single phone
