item.title: Watch your back Sony, Samsung’s ‘Galaxy Studio’ headphones are on the way — and these major leaks show them in all their glory
item.dc:content:
What you need to know

  • Samsung's rumored 'Galaxy Studio' headphones have been leaked once more, this time with visual components and animations
  • The footage points to ANC and Ambient sound modes, an 870mAh battery, head-tracking support, and other smart features
  • Unlike Sony, the Galaxy Studio headphones could sport both USB-C and 3.5mm ports for wired connectivity

Not since the release of 2014's Level Over headphones has Samsung stepped into the world of over-ear audio devices, and more leaks of its upcoming 'Galaxy Studio' headphones bring us one step closer to its potential unveiling.

We came across a wave of leaks back in October, where we first heard news that Samsung could challenge Sony and Apple with its own flagship headphones, but thanks to the eagle-eyed experts at SammyGuru, we now have illustrations and visual components that showcase the Galaxy Studio's versatile functions.

From what we know so far, design-wise, the Galaxy Studio headphones come in two shades (black or beige), with collapsible ear pads for travelling. The headphones are also projected to have an 870mAh battery.

Taking a page out of Sony's book

The reigning champion of our best wireless headphones, the Sony WH-1000 XM6 model, has clearly been an influence on the Galaxy Studio's development, but Samsung has also added its own flair to the device.

Just like its competitor, the Galaxy Studio packs most of its controls on the right ear pad. This supports touch gestures that trigger a multitude of functions, including tap to pause and play, double-tap to skip songs, triple-tap to go back, and there's even a touch-and-hold gesture that launches an AI assistant. It's pretty standard stuff for headphones, but the AI assistant integration gives it an extra boost.

As for its audio tools, it's more or less the same story. According to the animations leaked from the outlet, the Galaxy Studio has both Active Noise Canceling (ANC) and Ambient sound modes, with additional controls for ANC level, Ambient sound volume, and noise control level.

Just like Sony's range of over-ear headphones, it's likely that the Galaxy Studio will pack head tracking support, allowing spatial audio to adjust as you move your head. The headphones are expected to have an auto power-off tool where, if no audio is playing, the device turns off after a set period of time. In the APK, Samsung lists options for 30-minute, 60-minute, or 120-minute timeframe settings.

On top of this, the left ear pad will sport volume buttons, which Sony's flagship headphones don't have. Instead, you can adjust audio volume by vertically swiping up or down on the left ear pad.

Samsung goes one step further

As mentioned, the Galaxy Studio model will mark Samsung's first over-ear headphones release in 12 years, and between then and now, the audio game has changed drastically across the board among tech giants.

Of course, Samsung needs to take a couple of pages from the books of its rivals to play catch-up, but it's also focused on developing its own flagship features — most notably its versatile connectivity.

In addition to its audio functions, the leaks point to two separate ports (USB-C and 3.5mm), which allow you to connect the Galaxy Studio headphones to a mobile device for wired listening. This is a connectivity feature that Sony has yet to integrate into its own audio hardware lineup.

Listening wirelessly via Bluetooth is convenient, but true audiophiles know that wired listening is the best way to bring out the lossless and hi-res quality of digital music streaming. That said, the leaks don't detail how much the Galaxy Studio headphones reduce latency, the USB audio bit depth, or sample rate, so it'll take a series of hands-on experiences to determine how the headphones perform in that department.

The most frustrating part is that, at the end of the day, the headphones are still in development, so whether or not some of these specs make it into the final product is another story. But if everything lines up according to what we've seen so far, I fear that Sony, Apple, and Bose alike will start shaking in their boots.
item.description: Samsung's return to headphones is long overdue, and the rumored Galaxy Studio model is looking quite sharp on the specs front.

item.title: Vivo's next X Fold has a conundrum—there's a chip battle, and only one will win
item.dc:content:
Vivo is working on another foldable after debuting the X Fold 6 this past summer. Rumors suggest the Chinese OEM faces a decision: which chip to use.

This week, rumors on Weibo from tipster Digital Chat Station (DCS) suggest that Vivo's early X Fold 7 development has reached an important junction (via GSMArena). Here's where things get interesting—competition is the key ingredient. DCS suggests that Vivo's next foldable has been progressing well; however, the device is being tested with two chips in mind. These chips are from MediaTek and Qualcomm.

DCS claims Vivo is testing the Fold 7 with MediaTek's Dimensity 9600 Pro and Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite/Elite Extreme. Remember that the Elite Extreme is geared more toward "Ultra-level" phones, but that's neither here nor there. The tipster adds that Vivo might not consider specs and power for its X Fold 7 SoC.

Instead, the Chinese OEM could look at which company offers the most "competitive pricing." The tipster mentions one other aspect of this phone: its screen ratio.

DCS claims Vivo is moving forward with a "standard screen ratio" in mind. For comparison, imagine the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra—that's the general feel.

Spoiled for choice

Funnily enough, we've broken down these two chips from MediaTek and Qualcomm and put them head-to-head. Both chips utilize the latest 2nm process, and they're pretty darn similar—two sides of the same coin, if you will. Each chip's CPU capabilities are impressive. For the GPU, both Qualcomm and MediaTek have made strides in improving the graphics performance mobile devices can achieve. This should be a boon to gamers looking to play Wuthering Waves or NTE or another intensive game.

With that in mind, it feels like Vivo is spoiled for choice (it kind of is). The X Fold 6 launched this summer with MediaTek's Dimensity 9500 Super Edition. Before that, it settled with Qualcomm's Snapdragon.

item.title: Your foldable phone deserves better, and Google is making developers deliver
item.dc:content:
Google wants Android apps to do more than simply stretch across a bigger screen. Starting in April 2027, developers will have to meet new adaptive quality standards to keep their apps eligible for publishing and updates on Google Play.

The move adds to the pressure on developers to take foldable phones seriously and not to treat their larger displays as an afterthought. The new rules establish Tier 3, or Adaptive Ready, as the minimum requirement for standard apps. That means apps have to use the available screen without letterboxing or compatibility modes.

Google's announcement also says those apps must keep important information like scroll positions, text inputs, and media playback when users rotate, resize, fold, or unfold their devices. Support for multi-window environments is also mandatory.

The tech giant is also working to make store listings do more. Developers may already upload dedicated foldable screenshots in the Play Console, but from April 2027 new apps and app updates will be required to upload three foldable screenshots, on top of the usual two phone screenshots. These should be of the app running on different foldable screen configurations: square 1:1 inner displays, 4:3 inner displays, and folded outer screens.

Apart from basic compatibility, Google has two higher-quality tiers for developers willing to put in extra work. Tier 2, or Adaptive Optimized, includes support for accessories like keyboards, mice, trackpads, and styluses and responsive multi-pane layouts. Tier 1, or Adaptive Differentiated, goes even further, adding support for tabletop and book postures, camera continuity, interactive picture-in-picture, and multiple app instances.

There’s something for developers in it too. Apps that reach Tier 1 or Tier 2 are eligible for premium Play Store badges, improved merchandising, and editorial features. In essence, Google is trading more visibility for apps that make better use of expensive hardware.

Games have a slightly different timeline and expectations. Foldable screenshots become mandatory in April, and its Tier 3 requirements kick in starting in August 2027. Higher tiers will also consider graphics quality, performance, controller support, and frame-rate stability.

Developers will also have to keep an eye out for another deadline, as new and updated apps must target Android 17’s API level 37 by August 2027. Google also plans to bring its adaptive quality framework to tablets, Googlebooks and Android XR devices.
